chapter: New Orleans ballrooms and Tony Almerico
title: Growing up near Tony Almerico and hearing him practice
summary: Jones heard Almerico practicing as a neighborhood kid before playing trumpet, later working for him and finding him generous and kind.

story.theme_name: Remembering the early trumpeters and their styles
story.community_name: Trumpeters I admired: rating the horn players

blocks.x: Yeah. Yeah, that's the reason I brought it up, because I know your father was associated with the Jung. I crashed a few dances up there. Yeah, you were young and you could get in. Back to that neighborhood, when we left off, I guess it was last time, we were talking about Tony Almarico and how close you lived to him. So when you were a kid did you go to his house?

No, no. I can remember as a kid hearing Tony practice, running scales from scale after scale after scale. That was before I even played trumpet. We'd be, you know, kids played around the neighborhood and everything, I can remember, hearing him play in the afternoon, whether he'd be warming up or just keeping his chops up or between jobs, I don't know. But Tony did not know me from the neighborhood. By the time I started playing in the Parisian Room we had moved out of the neighborhood just a matter of a year or so before that. We had moved out to the lakefront, to Lake Vista, and lived out there. So he didn't know me from the neighborhood, you know, a neighborhood full of kids.
Yeah. But he was an important grown man in your eyes. Oh yes, oh yeah.

Well he had that mystique, he was a musician, a professional musician too. A guy that did it all the time. But we later spoke about, you know, I told him about how I used to listen to him when I was a kid and played. He couldn't even get a kick out of that. Tony was genuinely nice. He was just one of the most giving people that I've ever met in my life. He was just a warm, friendly, just a good man. And he did an awful lot for me and an awful lot for other people too. He's responsible for a lot of people being in the music business today. People who would not necessarily have had the chance to play and be heard. What did you call him? For a long time it was Mr. El Morico. Of course, the days were different in those days. Anyone who was older than you was Mr. and if you grew up with them, I would have had the time to play. And then it became, for some reason, another Nina, which is what? That's Italian. Yeah. I mean, like our nickname.
Yeah. Well, Nina Piconi is really not Nina. Never Tony though, huh? No, not that I can remember. But for a long time it was Mr. El Morico. Of course, the days were different in those days.
